Preprint.
TGR-EVODAG: A DAG-BASED MULTI-AGENT CODE
EVOLUTION FRAMEWORK FOR GENERATIVE RECOM-
MENDATION ON TENCENT
Junlin He1,2,*,
Junzhang Zhu1,*,
Yudong Li1,*,
Yihong Tang3,
Xuefeng Jiang4,
Wei Ma2,
Chengxiang Zhuo1,
Zang Li1
1Platform and Content Group, Tencent, Shenzhen, China
2The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, China
3McGill University, Montreal, Canada
4Independent Researcher, China
ABSTRACT
Large Language Model (LLM) agents have enabled automated code evolution,
offering a promising paradigm for algorithm discovery. However, current recursive
self-improvement (RSI) research for sequential recommendation faces a critical
dilemma: general-purpose code evolution frameworks possess flexible search
mechanisms but lack domain-specific feedback, whereas recommender-specific
evolution frameworks utilize rich feedback but rely on linear evolution. More
critically, naively integrating them fails when applied to Generative Recommenda-
tion (GR). Unlike traditional end-to-end models, GR relies on a module-cascaded
training pipeline (i.e., tokenization, pre-training, and alignment). In this paradigm,
existing naive evolution methods inevitably suffer from i) cost blindness: squan-
dering budgets by ignoring stage-asymmetric retraining overheads; and ii) short-
sighted evaluation: discarding promising upstream innovations that temporarily
regress metrics before downstream adaptation. To bridge these gaps, we propose
TGR-EvoDAG, a multi-agent code evolution framework explicitly tailored for
GR. TGR-EvoDAG organizes code evolution as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)
that explicitly maintains multiple evolution branches and merges complementary
innovations, and harmonizes an advanced search mechanism with rich GR-specific
diagnostic feedback. We further introduce stage-aware cost planning to optimize
real-world GPU-hour budgets, and active downstream co-adaptation to navigate
temporary regressions and unlock deferred cross-stage gains. On public Amazon
datasets, TGR-EvoDAG marks the first autonomous evolution of a complete GR
pipeline, improving offline metrics by up to 37.4% and boosting Agent4Rec sim-
ulated user satisfaction by 19.7% over the strongest GR baseline. Furthermore,
in industrial settings, the evolved GR achieves a 12.16% relative improvement in
offline Hit@1 and, when deployed as an additional retrieval channel on Tencent’s
large-scale commercial media platform, a statistically significant 0.40% increase in
online click-through rate (CTR).
1
INTRODUCTION
With the emergence of Large Language Model (LLM) agents, LLM-driven code evolution has
emerged as a promising paradigm, paving the way for Recursive Self-Improvement (Romera-Paredes
et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). This approach gives agents research-like capabilities:
they propose hypotheses, modify code, run experiments, and collect feedback, enabling algorithms
to self-evolve continuously (Lu et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026;
Chen et al., 2021). To accelerate experimental iterations and reduce labor costs for recommendation
engineers, an increasing number of studies have introduced this paradigm into the field of sequential
recommendation (Wang et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026; Mu et al., 2026).
While general-purpose code evolution has achieved sophisticated search mechanisms, such as multi-
branch exploration and cross-branch merging, through population-based approaches (Romera-Paredes

Figure 1: Comparison of recommendation paradigms and evolution framework capabilities. (a)
Traditional sequential recommendation relies on an end-to-end architecture characterized by uniform
retraining costs and immediate metric feedback. (b) GR utilizes a cascaded pipeline, which introduces
stage-asymmetric retraining costs and deferred cross-stage gains, causing existing frameworks to
suffer from cost blindness and short-sighted evaluation. (c) Capability comparison demonstrating
that TGR-EvoDAG uniquely fulfills the specific demands required to evolve cascaded GR pipelines.
et al., 2024; Lange et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2025) and tree/graph-based architectures (Jin et al.,
2026), they generally lack the domain-specific feedback signals essential for recommender systems.
Conversely, existing recommender evolution frameworks invest heavily in feedback quality by
utilizing simulated users and diagnostic probes, yet they predominantly rely on primitive search
mechanisms. For instance, SERS (Wang et al., 2026) uses a simple fan-out/fan-in strategy without
branch maintenance; EvoRec performs greedy, round-by-round linear advancement (Mu et al., 2026);
and Self-EvolveRec samples a parent node from multiple elites (Kim et al., 2026).
These simple search mechanisms restrict existing recommender evolution frameworks to traditional
end-to-end models, where modifications incur a uniform full-training cost and produce immediate
metric changes (Kang & McAuley, 2018; Hidasi et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2019). They fail on
Generative Recommendation (GR), an increasingly popular paradigm built on a cascaded pipeline
(tokenizer, pre-training, and alignment)(Geng et al., 2022; Rajput et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024;
Deng et al., 2025; Pang et al., 2025; TGR Team et al., 2026), because they cannot effectively maintain
or merge cross-stage innovations. While explicitly combining advanced general-purpose search
mechanisms with domain-specific feedback seems like a natural solution, this naive integration still
falls short. General-purpose mechanisms fundamentally rely on two implicit assumptions that a
cascaded GR pipeline structurally violates: 1) Cost Blindness vs. Stage-Dependent Costs. General-
purpose search policies evaluate all candidate nodes uniformly, ignoring how much retraining an
edit requires. In GR, however, retraining costs are highly asymmetric: modifying the upstream
Tokenizer forces a full-pipeline retraining, whereas editing the downstream Alignment stage only
re-runs the final segment. Being “cost-blind,” existing frameworks cannot triage edits based on
actual overhead, systematically squandering budgets on expensive upstream explorations. 2) Short-
Sighted Evaluation vs. Deferred Gains. General-purpose frameworks judge modifications by
their immediate scores, pruning candidates that initially regress performance. However, because
GR stages are tightly coupled, modifying an upstream stage almost always breaks compatibility
with the unadapted downstream stage, causing a temporary performance drop. Lacking structural
awareness, existing frameworks abandon these upstream innovations, missing the opportunity to
actively schedule the necessary downstream adaptations to unlock “deferred” gains(Liu et al., 2025a).
To this end, we present TGR-EvoDAG, a multi-agent code evolution framework explicitly built for
cascaded GR pipelines. TGR-EvoDAG seamlessly marries advanced graph search mechanisms with
rich domain-specific feedback. It represents the search space as a Code Directed Acyclic Graph
(Code DAG), driven by a five-stage collaborative Agent workflow (comprising an Operator Selector,
2


--- Page 3 ---
Preprint.
Architect-Critic, Coder-Reviewer, Distiller, and Pruner) that digests fine-grained recommendation
signals, such as mathematical probes and simulated user (Zhang et al., 2024). Building upon this
foundation, TGR-EvoDAG tightly integrates the multi-agent workflow with two novel mechanisms
to overcome the inherent blind spots of cascaded pipelines. First, to address cost blindness, we
introduce Stage-Aware Cost Planning via the Operator Selector. Each DAG node records the
exact pipeline stages its edit touches and the corresponding retraining overhead. Empowered by
this stage-aware schema, our Operator Selector dynamically balances the expected performance
gain against the actual GPU-hour cost, preventing the framework from blindly exhausting budgets
on expensive upstream explorations. Second, to overcome short-sighted evaluation, we design
Active Downstream Co-Adaptation. Instead of rigidly discarding candidates that cause immediate
performance drops, TGR-EvoDAG explicitly retains these seemingly “regressed” upstream branches.
When the framework identifies an upstream edit (e.g., Tokenizer) lacking a corresponding downstream
adaptation (e.g., Pre-training), the agents deliberately schedule a child node to adapt the downstream
stage. This recovers gains from upstream edits that greedy frameworks would discard.
To evaluate our framework fairly, we construct a standardized GR evolution platform equipped with
stage-aware feedback and precise GPU-hour accounting, ensuring all compared frameworks evolve
from an identical seed codebase. In summary, our core contributions are:
• We identify and formulate the structural mismatch between current code evolution frameworks and
cascaded GR pipelines. Specifically, we expose how cost blindness and short-sighted evaluation
cause existing methods to systematically misallocate computational budgets and discard promising
cross-stage innovations.
• We propose TGR-EvoDAG, which harmonizes Code DAG search mechanisms with domain-specific
feedback via a comprehensive five-stage multi-agent workflow. By further introducing stage-aware
cost planning and active co-adaptation, TGR-EvoDAG enables efficient GR evolution.
• We develop a standardized GR evolution platform. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TGR-
EvoDAG achieves the fully autonomous evolution of a complete GR training pipeline, surpassing
both general and recommender-specific evolutionary baselines. It improves offline metrics by up
to 37.4% and boosts user satisfaction in the Agent4Rec simulated environment by 19.7% over
the strongest GR baseline. Moreover, applying the evolved architecture to Tencent’s real-world
industrial scenarios yields a 12.16% relative improvement in offline Hit@1 and a statistically
significant 0.40% increase in online Click-Through Rate in a 14-day A/B test, demonstrating its
practical value.
TGR-EvoDAG is part of the TGR series of generative recommendation research at Tencent (TGR
Team et al., 2026). Beyond this paper, TGR-EvoDAG has been integrated into Tencent’s internal
Uppimo platform as its implementation backbone, which productizes the recursive self-improvement
(RSI) workflow described here for production recommendation teams; the platform will be made
available for public trial in the future.
2
RELATED WORK
LLM-driven Code Evolution. General-purpose code evolution relies on three search paradigms.
Linear inheritance advances a single thread (e.g., AIDE, MLE-STAR (Nam et al., 2025; Yang et al.,
2025; Guo et al., 2024)), often stalling at local optima. Multi-elite sampling draws parents from
elite archives to preserve diversity (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al.,
2026; Liu et al., 2025b; 2024; Ye et al., 2024). Explicit tree search maintains multiple branches for
persistent exploration (e.g., SELA, Arbor (Chi et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2026)); notably, CORAL (Qu
et al., 2026) even removes fixed strategies and delegates all search routing to the agent itself. Despite
their sophisticated search, these frameworks fail on Generative Recommendation (GR). First, they
lack the domain-specific feedback (e.g., mathematical probes, simulated users) essential for GR.
Second, facing GR’s cascaded pipeline, they lack stage-aware cost planning to handle asymmetric
retraining overheads, and cross-stage mechanisms to merge and co-adapt innovations from upstream
tokenization down to alignment.
Generative Recommendation (GR). GR replaces classical ID-based models (Hidasi et al., 2016;
Kang & McAuley, 2018; Sun et al., 2019) with direct semantic-ID generation (Tay et al., 2022;
3


--- Page 4 ---
Preprint.
Rajput et al., 2023). Training GR forms a cascaded three-stage pipeline: a Tokenizer quantizes items
into hierarchical IDs (Lee et al., 2022); Pre-training fits a sequence-to-sequence generator; and Post-
training aligns it with preference signals (Chen et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2025; OneRec Team, 2025; Yu
et al., 2026). Current manual research optimizes each stage locally, spanning better tokenizers (Zheng
et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2025), quantization (Fifty et al., 2025), and
architectures (Zhai et al., 2024). Because stage-wise improvements are complementary, the global
optimum hides in their combinations, a space no single-threaded search can cover. Furthermore,
these stages are tightly coupled (Liu et al., 2025a); upstream innovations often trigger temporary
metric drops, requiring downstream re-adaptation to unlock their delayed value. No prior work
autonomously evolves this complete pipeline.
Self-Evolving Recommender Systems. A nascent line applies code evolution to recommenders.
SERS (Wang et al., 2026), deployed in YouTube’s production system, evolves delta edits against a
fixed baseline via a simple fan-out/fan-in strategy. EvoRec (Mu et al., 2026) advances the model
architecture greedily, round by round, keeping only the single best variant at each step. Self-
EvolveRec (Kim et al., 2026) employs an LLM-based user simulator (Park et al., 2023; Zhang
et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), and samples a single parent from multiple elites. These frameworks
all introduce recommender-specific feedback signals, yet adopt a simple search mechanism that
maintains and merges no parallel branches. They fail when evolving a cascaded GR pipeline: its
complementary cross-stage gains must be merged to reach the global optimum, and its upstream
edits pay off only after downstream re-adaptation. Concurrently, Auto-RecSys (Li et al., 2026)
applies autonomous research agents to industry-scale recommender models. It focuses on engineering
orchestration for long-running experiments (persistent state, failure recovery, and human-in-the-loop
checkpoints), which is complementary to our work; its search advances each idea linearly, without
explicit GPU-hour budgeting, stage-aware cost planning, or cross-branch merging.
3
PRELIMINARIES
Let U and I denote the sets of users and items. In sequential recommendation, given a user’s
chronological interaction history Su, the objective is to predict the next item it+1. Generative
Recommendation (GR) reformulates this as a conditional sequence generation problem. It maps
items to discrete semantic identifiers (SIDs) and autoregressively generates the SID tokens of it+1
conditioned on Su. Training a GR model therefore involves three tightly coupled stages: (1) Stage I:
Tokenization. A tokenizer (e.g., RQ-VAE) discretizes item content into hierarchical semantic IDs.
(2) Stage II: Generative Pre-training. A sequence-to-sequence Transformer is trained to predict the
next item’s tokens via hierarchical cross-entropy. (3) Stage III: Post-training Alignment. The model
is further aligned with desired recommendation objectives (e.g., exact match or prefix similarity)
using preference optimization or reinforcement learning. We detail the concrete implementation
details and mathematical formulations of these three stages (e.g., RQ-Kmeans quantization, exact
baseline objectives, and post-training variants) to Appendix A.3.
4
TGR-EVODAG
We present TGR-EvoDAG, a multi-agent code evolution framework designed for the cascaded
training pipeline of generative recommendation. As shown in Figure 2, TGR-EvoDAG explicitly
represents the evolution history as a Code DAG. This representation enables the framework to preserve
multiple promising branches, revisit earlier pipeline stages, and semantically merge complementary
improvements discovered along different branches.
At evolution round t, the global search state is encapsulated as S(t) = (G(t), b(t)), where
G(t) = (V(t), E(t)) is the current Code DAG, and b(t) denotes the remaining evolution bud-
get. Each node vi ∈V(t) acts as a self-contained experimental record tracking three categories
of structured attributes: (1) Provenance, including the parent set Pi, applied search operator
oi ∈{EXPLORE, MUTATE, MERGE}, underlying hypothesis Hi, and branch status Qi; (2) Artifacts,
covering the incremental code modification ∆i, executable codebase snapshot Bi, and associated
artifacts Ai (e.g., vocabularies, checkpoints); and (3) Empirical Execution, storing the validation
feedback Fi, distilled lessons Di, and consumed experimental cost Ci. The edge set is naturally
induced by developmental dependencies, E(t) = {(u, vi) | vi ∈V(t), u ∈Pi}. Because each new

node is derived exclusively from previously evaluated nodes and never modifies its ancestry, G(t) is

4.1
SEARCH OPERATORS
TGR-EvoDAG transitions the search state by applying one of three search operators to generate a
new child node vc. These operators determine the parent set Pc and dictate the semantic instructions
delivered to the multi-agent system.
Exploration.
Exploration branches out from a single parent node (Pc = {vp}) to investigate a
fundamentally different direction. Agents formulate a novel hypothesis Hc distinct from its ancestry,
such as introducing a new training objective, changing the user-conditioning architecture, or applying
a different post-training algorithm.
Mutation.
Mutation performs exploitation and local refinement on a single parent node (Pc =
{vp}). Agents keep the core hypothesis of vp intact while performing localized optimizations, such
as adjusting loss weights, tuning hyperparameters, or modifying sampling strategies.
Merge.
The MERGE operator synthesizes complementary improvements discovered across multiple
independent branches (Pc = {vp1, . . . , vpr}, r ≥2). Unlike single-parent operators, MERGE
aggregates a multi-dimensional context. The framework packages the hypotheses, codebases, and
validation feedback of all parent nodes and forwards them to the pipeline. Agents are tasked to
identify complementary mechanisms, resolve semantic code conflicts or interface dependencies, and
integrate them into a unified functional codebase Bc under a synergized hypothesis Hc. To keep the
context tractable, we do not inject full codebase snapshots; instead, each parent is serialized as a
unified diff against the lowest common ancestor in the DAG. Each diff is paired with its structured
hypothesis H and distilled lessons D. This representation stays within the context window while
preserving the information needed to resolve cross-branch conflicts.
5


--- Page 6 ---
Preprint.
4.2
MULTI-AGENT PIPELINE
Each node expansion is executed by a five-stage pipeline instantiated by seven specialized LLM
agents: an Operator Selector, an Architect-Critic pair, a Coder-Reviewer pair, a Distiller, and a Pruner.
To ensure rigorous evolution, agents communicate through structured intermediate records (e.g.,
JSON schemas) rather than unconstrained natural language. The complete workflow is summarized
in Algorithm 1 (Appendix A.1).
Stage-Aware Cost Planning via Operator Selector.
Instead of simply counting search itera-
tions, TGR-EvoDAG manages a realistic GPU-hour budget b(t) via empirical cost profiling. Every
evaluated node explicitly records the actual time spent on each pipeline stage (e.g., Tokenizer, Pre-
training, Alignment). Provided with these historical records, the Operator Selector specifies the
target_stage and training_scope of its intended edit using a structured JSON schema.
This allows the system to estimate the expected GPU-hour cost Cc before execution. By weighing
this expected cost against anticipated performance gains, the Operator Selector makes strategic
budgeting decisions. For instance, it deliberately postpones expensive upstream edits (which force
full-pipeline retraining) until cheaper downstream architectures fully mature, preventing premature
budget exhaustion.
Hypothesis development.
Conditioned on the selected operator oc and parents Pc, the Architect
formulates the hypothesis Hc as a structured blueprint detailing the diagnosed limitation, proposed
mechanism, affected stages, expected diagnostic changes, and potential risks. The Critic then
evaluates this blueprint against historical lessons and graph ancestry to verify logical consistency and
ensure measurable effects. They engage in an iterative refinement loop until the hypothesis passes all
structural and semantic checks.
Implementation and review.
Guided by Hc, the Coder implements the codebase snapshot Bc in an
isolated workspace initialized from the parents. The Coder and Reviewer execute a multi-round repair
loop informed by static analysis and peer review. The Reviewer verifies that the implementation
faithfully realizes the blueprint, preserves the evaluation protocol without data leakage, and maintains
cross-stage compatibility. For MERGE nodes, it additionally ensures mechanisms inherited from
all branches remain functionally active. This loop terminates when the candidate passes all tests or
exhausts the repair budget.
Evaluation and lesson distillation.
The standardized environment executes compiled candidates
and returns a comprehensive feedback object Fc, encapsulating validation metrics, mathematical
probes, user diagnostic reports, and consumed computational costs. The Distiller then analyzes the
hypothesis Hc, the code delta ∆c, and the empirical feedback Fc to synthesize mechanism-level
lessons Dc. These lessons explicitly record the tested mechanism, supporting evidence, applicable
conditions, and failure attributes.
Search control and active co-adaptation.
After evaluating vc, the Pruner acts as a search router
rather than a simple filter. Jointly analyzing quantitative metrics and the Distiller’s lessons Dc, the
Pruner dynamically dictates branch state transitions via structured outputs. First, for paths with
irrecoverable collapses, it assigns a [Pruned] state, masking them from the Operator Selector
to conserve computation. Second, to address cascaded pipelines, it enables active downstream
co-adaptation. When an upstream innovation (e.g., Tokenizer edit) causes a metric regression due
to cross-stage incompatibility, the Pruner emits a [Needs-Downstream-Adaptation] tag.
Subsequent Operator Selector prompts are strictly conditioned on these tags, forcing the system to
freeze upstream parameters and mutate the downstream architecture. Consequently, tightly coupled
cross-stage mechanisms are co-evolved rather than prematurely discarded.
5
EXPERIMENTS
In this section, we conduct numerical experiments to answer five research questions. (RQ1): Does
code-level DAG evolution with domain-specific feedback beat both general and recommender-specific
evolutionary frameworks? (RQ2): Does stage-aware cost planning overcome cost blindness and
6


--- Page 7 ---
Preprint.
budget for expensive upstream (Tokenizer) innovations? (RQ3): Do active downstream co-adaptation
and cross-branch merging overcome short-sighted evaluation? (RQ4): Can the evolved architecture
transfer to real-world industrial scenarios? (RQ5): Are user diagnosis and mathematical probes
causally useful in driving mutations?
Setup and Protocol.
All frameworks evolve on a unified platform under a fixed budget B = 24
GPU-hours, using Claude CLI (Liu et al., 2026) with all inference routed to GLM-5.2 (GLM-5-Team
et al., 2026), starting from an identical TIGER seed codebase (plus post-training variants SDPO,
SPRec, ReReGRPO, APAO) on the Amazon Office Products dataset. The final champion architecture
evolved on this public dataset is subsequently transferred to Tencent’s large-scale industrial platform
for real-world validation (Section 5). We compare against general frameworks (AlphaEvolve (Novikov
et al., 2025), DeepEvolve (Liu et al., 2025b), CORAL (Qu et al., 2026), Arbor (Jin et al., 2026))
and recommender-specific ones (EvoRec (Mu et al., 2026), Self-EvolveRec (Kim et al., 2026));
detailed configurations of the datasets, codebases, and baselines are provided in Appendix A.2, A.3,
A.4. The platform exposes three feedback channels: (i) offline metrics (Hit@K/NDCG@K), (ii)
deterministic mathematical probes, and (iii) LLM-based user diagnosis (Appendix A.5). Standard
general baselines receive only offline metrics channel (i), whereas recommender-specific frameworks
(EvoRec, Self-EvolveRec) and TGR-EvoDAG access all three channels. To strictly decouple the
benefit of diagnostic feedback from evolutionary search topology, we further construct two naive
integration baselines, namely CORAL + Diag. and Arbor + Diag., which augment the strongest
general search frameworks with identical multi-channel feedback. Model selection uses offline
validation metrics alone. Both user diagnostic reports and Agent4Rec simulations are driven by
DeepSeek-v4-flash(DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) with a temperature of 0 to ensure determinism and
reproducibility. Crucially, evolutionary user diagnosis samples 50 simulated users, whereas post hoc
Agent4Rec metrics (Zhang et al., 2024) are evaluated on 100 separate simulated users, keeping the
two user cohorts strictly disjoint and non-overlapping to avoid evaluation leakage (Appendix A.6).
Main Results.
As shown in Table 1, we make the following observations. (1) Consistent domi-
nance. TGR-EvoDAG leads on every metric, improving over the strongest non-evolutionary baseline
APAO by +24.7%/+28.5% on Hit@10/@20 and +37.4%/+37.2% on NDCG@10/@20. (2) Dis-
entangling domain feedback from search topology. A critical question is whether the gains of
TGR-EvoDAG stem simply from richer feedback or from its DAG-based evolutionary mechanisms.
Comparing Arbor with Arbor + Diag. confirms that domain diagnostics indeed help (Hit@10 increases
from 0.0792 to 0.0814). However, naively integrating domain feedback into general tree-based or
population-based frameworks remains suboptimal: TGR-EvoDAG still significantly outperforms
Arbor + Diag. (+6.8% Hit@10, +16.9% NDCG@10) and CORAL + Diag. (+8.1% Hit@10,
+16.0% NDCG@10). This empirical gap demonstrates that feedback richness alone cannot substi-
tute for structural search capabilities: without DAG-based cross-branch merging and stage-aware
cost planning, general search frameworks fail to afford upstream tokenizer retraining or overcome
temporary regressions during downstream co-adaptation. Furthermore, TGR-EvoDAG beats the
strongest domain-specific baseline Self-EvolveRec by +21.0% Hit@10 / +32.8% NDCG@10 due to
its multi-branch exploration. (3) Offline and simulated experience move together. Beyond offline
metrics, the Agent4Rec leaps (View +31.3%, Satisfaction +19.7%, Depth +25.4% over APAO)
confirm that the discovered architectures yield genuinely better recommendations, answering RQ1.
Analysis of Evolution Trajectory (RQ1-RQ3).
Figure 3 illustrates the 39-round evolution tra-
jectory from the initial TIGER seed (Hit@10 0.0626) to the final architecture (0.0869) across five
distinct phases, directly answering RQ1–RQ3. (Phase 1) The framework first establishes a robust
baseline by injecting both collaborative and semantic IDs into the TIGER encoder, adjusting InfoNCE
weights, and grid-searching feature fusion and user pooling methods (0.0626→0.0673). (Phase 2)
Next, TGR-EvoDAG opens multiple orthogonal branches based on diagnostic signals. This DAG
structure safely explores and deepens parallel mutations (e.g., recency bias, user-conditional decod-
ing) without destabilizing the main trunk, demonstrating a clear advantage over linear frameworks
(RQ1). (Phase 3) It then pairwise merges these independently matured branches and stacks them with
APAO, creating a single-step performance leap to 0.0824 (+12.3%) and validating the effectiveness
of cross-branch merging (RQ3). (Phase 4) Because modifying the upstream tokenizer requires
expensive full-pipeline retraining, TGR-EvoDAG strategically defers this to avoid budget waste. It
tests the new Repr-LLM encoder on an isolated branch, where introducing PSRQ initially causes a

trunk integration, demonstrating how stage-aware cost planning overcomes cost blindness (RQ2).
(Phase 5) Finally, when this repaired tokenizer is merged into the main trunk, performance initially
regresses to 0.0775. Instead of discarding it via greedy search, TGR-EvoDAG retains the node and
actively co-adapts downstream components by re-tuning the fine-margin loss. This successfully
recovers performance, pushing the model to its final peak of 0.0869 after a final merge with the
APAO branch, thereby overcoming short-sighted evaluation (RQ3).

Ablation of Search Mechanisms (RQ2 & RQ3).
We re-evolve under restricted variants: A (greedy:
no multi-branch, prunes any regression), B (multi-elite but no cross-branch merge), and C (full search
but without cost planning, uniform budget across stages). As shown in Figure 4(a,b), performance
rises monotonically from A to Full TGR-EvoDAG on both testset and Agent4Rec metrics. A stalls
at a local optimum, as its short-sighted greedy pruning cannot survive the temporary regressions
required for downstream co-adaptation. B tolerates these delayed payoffs but remains blind to the
compounding gains of merging independent branches, answering RQ3. C adds merging but suffers
from cost blindness; lacking stage-aware planning, it exhausts the budget uniformly and cannot afford
the expensive upstream tokenizer retraining. Full TGR-EvoDAG finally triages its budget properly to
conquer the upstream stage, unlocking the terminal peak and answering RQ2.

Figure 4: Ablation of search mechanisms and industrial evaluation. (a) Testset metrics and (b)
Agent4Rec metrics under restricted search variants (A: greedy; B: multi-elite; C: w/o cost planning)
versus Full TGR-EvoDAG, where performance rises monotonically from A to Full. (c) Real-world
industrial offline evaluation of the evolved GR pipeline over the APAO baseline across Hit@K.
Real-World Industrial Deployment (RQ4).
We deploy the champion GR architecture to Tencent’s
commercial media platform with over 10 million daily active users. This deployment is carried out
through Tencent’s internal Uppimo platform, into which TGR-EvoDAG has been integrated as its core
evolution engine. The production system follows a standard retrieval-pre-ranking-ranking cascade.
Offline Transferability. We train the champion architecture and the strongest baseline APAO from
scratch using 10 days of industrial logs (>10 million interactions). As shown in Figure 4(c), our
evolved model strictly improves over APAO across all metrics(+12.16% Hit@1, +4.83% Hit@5,
+0.25% Hit@50). Online A/B Testing. We subsequently deployed the evolved model as a novel
retrieval channel for a 14-day A/B test on 5% of live traffic (serving >1M users). To ensure strict
statistical rigor, we applied CUPED variance reduction and controlled the false discovery rate via
tiered Benjamini-Hochberg correction (q ≤0.05). The online results reveal a significant overall
system CTR increase of +0.40% (p = 0.019). Furthermore, the new channel contributes over
10% of unique exposures (relevant items completely missed by existing channels) and achieves a
channel-specific CTR ≈13% higher than the system average.
Validation of Diagnostic Signals (RQ5).
To answer whether diagnostic signals are causally
useful in driving mutations, we highlight three critical turning points where offline metrics alone
offered no actionable direction. (i) User Diagnosis: When performance plateaued, simulated user
feedback explicitly reported that recommendations were “outdated,” motivating the agent to inject
an exponential recency bias. When an initial weak prior (γ=0.9) showed no offline improvement,
diagnostics confirmed it was absorbed by learnable weights, prompting the agent to apply a stronger
signal (γ=0.5) that successfully broke the plateau. (ii) Mathematical Probes: Standard metrics only
indicate overall correctness, but mathematical probes isolated a specific “same coarse, wrong fine”
error mode. This directly drove the agent to design a targeted within-coarse hard-negative contrastive
loss that random mutation could not easily discover. (iii) Distribution Probes: When the new PSRQ
tokenizer caused a catastrophic performance drop, an offline-only search would have discarded it.
However, distribution probes pinpointed a semantic ID collision spike (to 65.7%) due to a k-means
scale imbalance. This causal insight guided the agent to apply an RMS normalization repair, dropping
collisions back to 1.0% and unlocking the tokenizer’s potential. Ultimately, while offline metrics
only flag failures, these diagnostics provide the exact causal mechanisms required for the agent to
execute targeted repairs.
9


--- Page 10 ---
Preprint.
6
CONCLUSION
In this paper, we introduce TGR-EvoDAG, a multi-agent code evolution framework tailored for
Generative Recommendation (GR). We observe that naively integrating existing evolution frameworks
fails on GR’s cascaded pipelines due to two fundamental bottlenecks: cost blindness and short-sighted
evaluation. To bridge this gap, TGR-EvoDAG harmonizes an advanced Code Directed Acyclic Graph
(Code DAG) search mechanism with rich diagnostic feedback. Building upon this foundation, it
introduces stage-aware cost planning to explicitly triage edits based on actual GPU overhead, and
active downstream co-adaptation to safely navigate temporary regressions and unlock deferred gains.
Extensive evaluations on a standardized GR platform demonstrate that TGR-EvoDAG achieves
state-of-the-art performance, outperforming the leading non-evolutionary baseline (APAO) by up to
37.4% in offline metrics and 19.7% in simulated user satisfaction. In addition, successful migration to
Tencent’s real-world industrial scenarios yields a 12.16% relative improvement in offline Hit@1 and
a statistically significant 0.40% gain in online Click-Through Rate. Moving forward, building on its
integration into Tencent’s Uppimo platform, we plan to directly evolve GR pipelines within complex
industrial scenarios and to open the platform for public trial. Moreover, since Large Language Model
(LLM) training inherently involves cascaded stages, we envision our framework can be naturally
extended to optimize multi-stage LLM pipelines.

AI USE STATEMENT
In this work, we used generative AI tools only for tasks with recommended disclosure. Specifically,
(1) we used a large language model to assist in reading and summarizing prior baseline works to aid
our own understanding of the related literature, and (2) we used a large language model to polish the
writing (grammar, phrasing, and clarity) of the manuscript. We did not use generative AI tools for
any tasks with required disclosure: the research ideas, the proposed TGR-EvoDAG framework and its
algorithms, the experimental design, and all code and experiments were conceived and implemented
by the authors. Data generation and other required-disclosure tasks are not applicable to this work.
We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. All AI-generated summaries of baseline methods were cross-
checked by the authors against the original papers to ensure factual accuracy, and all AI-polished
text was manually verified by the authors to preserve the intended technical meaning. We take full
responsibility for the final content of this work, including all text, claims, and artifacts.

A
APPENDIX
A.1
WORKFLOW
Algorithm 1 expands a single evolution round of TGR-EvoDAG. We present the round in the same five
stages as Section 4.2, and use this section to make precise what the main text states only qualitatively:
the records exchanged between the agents, the accounting of the budget b(t), and the transition of the
branch status Q.
Agent records.
Each agent is invoked as a single call constrained to one structured record, which
the harness parses directly; a response that cannot be parsed is discarded and the call is repeated
rather than repaired, so that no free-form residue enters the node attributes and every intermediate
decision remains machine-checkable. The Operator Selector consumes the serialised graph G(t)
together with the remaining budget b(t) and returns the operator oc and parent set Pc; the Architect
consumes these and the ancestral lessons and returns the hypothesis Hc; the Coder and Reviewer
consume Hc and return the codebase snapshot Bc with the delta ∆c; the Distiller consumes Hc, ∆c,
and the feedback Fc and returns the lesson Dc; and the Pruner consumes Fc, Dc, oc, and the touched
stage and returns the branch status Qc. Two of these choices are deliberate. The Critic is instructed
to reject a blueprint only when it violates a hard invariant, cannot yield an executable forward pass,
is a no-op, or re-proposes a direction already falsified without addressing the recorded lesson Di; a
rejected blueprint costs a full round of agent calls, whereas an accepted but unpromising one costs
only a single evaluation, so the asymmetry favours acceptance. The Distiller is given the Coder’s
workspace together with (Hc, ∆c, Fc) and inspects ∆c before writing Dc, so that a lesson attributes
the outcome to a mechanism (a specific layer, objective, or initialization) instead of restating Hc.
Budget accounting.
A round is charged the GPU-hours measured by the environment, Cc, and
not the expected cost estimated from the target_stage and training_scope attributes. That
estimate only informs the Operator Selector’s strategic decision; the decrement b(t+1) ←b(t) −Cc
always uses the measured value, which is recovered stage by stage and stored on the node, so that
the cost profile available to later rounds reflects the true stage-asymmetric overheads of the pipeline.
A round that fails review or is interrupted before yielding a usable candidate is charged τfail, the
GPU-hours spent before the failure, so that repeatedly proposing unexecutable candidates cannot be
used to explore at no cost. Token consumption is logged separately and does not draw on b(t).
Branch-status transition.
A node that passes review and yields a valid checkpoint, whether or
not it improves on its parent, keeps its default status and remains selectable, since an immediate
regression on an upstream edit is precisely the signal that downstream co-adaptation is required.
Only the two tagged statuses alter the search: [Pruned] is assigned on an irrecoverable collapse
(unexecutable or protocol-violating code, a broken item↔code mapping, or a metric collapse with
no diagnostic route) and removes the subtree permanently, masking it from the Operator Selector;
[Needs-Downstream-Adaptation] is assigned when a metric regression is caused by an
upstream (tokenization or pre-training) edit and conditions the subsequent Operator Selector prompts
so that upstream parameters are frozen and the child node must mutate the downstream stage to
restore cross-stage compatibility.
16


--- Page 17 ---
Preprint.
Algorithm 1 TGR-EvoDAG
Require: Seed codebase B0, maximum GPU-hour budget B, standardized environment E, failure
penalty τfail
Ensure: The best candidate node selected by validation performance
1: Initialize root node v0 containing B0
2: Initialize global graph G(0) = ({v0}, ∅)
3: t ←0, b(0) ←B
4: while b(t) > 0 do
5:

6:

7:
# 2. Hypothesis Development
8:
Hc ←ARCHITECTCRITIC(Pc, oc, G(t))
9:
# 3. Implementation and Review
10:
Bc, ∆c ←CODERREVIEWER(Hc, Pc, oc)
11:
# 4. Evaluation and Lesson Distillation
12:
if Bc passes review and is executable then
13:
Fc, tokenst, Cc ←EVALUATE(Bc, E)
# Cc is the actual GPU-hour cost
14:
else
15:
Fc ←Failure feedback, tokenst ←Debugging cost, Cc ←τfail
# measured GPU-hours
spent before failure
16:
end if
17:
LOG(tokenst)
# Track LLM token consumption
18:
Dc ←DISTILL(Hc, ∆c, Fc)
19:
# 5. Search Control and Active Co-Adaptation
20:
Construct child node vc with attributes (Pc, oc, Hc, ∆c, Bc, Fc, Dc, Cc, . . . )
21:
Add vc and derivation edges to form intermediate graph G′
22:
state, stage ←PRUNER(Fc, Dc, oc)
# stage: touched pipeline stage read from Hc
23:
if state == DEAD_END then
24:
Mark vc as [Pruned]
25:
else if state == METRIC_DROP AND stage == UPSTREAM then
26:
Mark vc as [Needs-Downstream-Adaptation]
27:
end if
28:
G(t+1) ←UpdateGraph(G′, vc)
29:
Update remaining budget: b(t+1) ←b(t) −Cc
30:
t ←t + 1
31: end while
32: return arg maxvi∈V ValidationMetric(Fi)

A.2
DATASETS
In this section, we introduce the open-source Amazon Office dataset used for evolution, as well as
the industrial dataset used to verify whether the evolved GR architecture is effective in real-world
industrial scenarios.
Amazon Office Dataset. Following the evaluation protocol of the initial codebase (Yu et al., 2026) and
prior generative recommendation studies (Rajput et al., 2023), we conduct all evolution experiments
on the Office Products category of the public Amazon Product Review corpus1. We directly adopt
the preprocessed data released by Yu et al. (2026). For completeness, we restate the protocol under
which the released data were produced: each review is treated as one implicit positive interaction,
and every user’s interactions are sorted chronologically into a single behaviour sequence. Five-core
filtering then iteratively discards users and items with fewer than five interactions. Each history is
truncated to the most recent 20 items. Finally, the data is split with the standard leave-one-out strategy.
For every user, the chronologically last interaction forms the test instance, the second-to-last forms
the validation instance, and the rest are used for training. All evolutionary frameworks therefore
optimise and are selected on exactly the same validation split, and the test split is touched only once,
for the final checkpoint selected within the budget B. Item side information (title, brand, category,
price and description) is concatenated into a textual description and used exclusively by the item
tokenizer. The statistics of the released data are summarised in Table 2. Let U, I and D denote the
user set, the item set and the interaction set, respectively. We report the average sequence length
L = |D|/|U| and the interaction density ρ = |D|

(|U| × |I|).
Table 2: Statistics of the Amazon Office dataset. We directly use the preprocessed data released
by Yu et al. (2026), obtained under five-core filtering and leave-one-out splitting.
Dataset
|U|
|I|
|D|
L
ρ
Amazon Office
4,905
2,420
53,258
10.86
0.45%
We deliberately select Office as the evolution dataset rather than a larger benchmark. This is because
a compact corpus keeps a single train/validate cycle below one GPU-hour, so that the unified budget
of B = 24 GPU-hours admits a meaningful number of evolution rounds for every framework.
Real-world Industrial Dataset. The industrial data are collected from Tencent’s large-scale com-
mercial media platform with over 10 million daily active users. The production model is trained
continuously on streaming logs. For a controlled offline comparison, all models are trained on the
same 10 consecutive days of logs (over 10 million interactions on more than 300 thousand items)
and evaluated on the following day. A positive interaction is a click. The item text fed to the tok-
enizer concatenates textual metadata (e.g., title, category, and tags) with a caption of the item image
generated by a multimodal LLM. User histories are truncated to the 500 most recent interactions.
The platform serves recommendations through a retrieval–pre-ranking–ranking cascade, in which the
evolved GR model is added as one retrieval channel for the online A/B test (Section 5). Exact user
and item counts and absolute CTR values are withheld for confidentiality.
A.3
GR CODEBASE
In this section, we introduce the codebase provided for the evolutionary framework.
All frameworks evolve upon an identical seed codebase, which is built directly on the officially
released APAO implementation (Yu et al., 2026) together with its preprocessed data and its original
tokenizer configuration. The codebase is organised into four decoupled modules: (i) item tokenization,
(ii) backbone definition, (iii) the pre-training objective, and (iv) a pluggable post-training objective.
All four share one data loader and one beam-search evaluator. What is held invariant across all
frameworks is the environment: the preprocessed interaction data, the train/validation/test split, the
evaluation protocol and the budget B. Everything above the data layer, including the tokenization
module, is exposed as mutable code and may be modified by a candidate during evolution.
1https://jmcauley.ucsd.edu/data/amazon/links.html
18


--- Page 19 ---
Preprint.
Item Tokenization. Every item is represented by a sequence of discrete semantic tokens rather than
a single atomic ID. The seed codebase ships with the tokenizer configuration of Yu et al. (2026):
a semantic embedding is first extracted for each item by feeding its concatenated textual metadata
into LLAMA-3.1-8B-INSTRUCT and taking the final-layer representation; a 4-level RQ-K-means
quantizer then residually quantizes each embedding into T = 4 codes (y1, y2, y3, y4), one per level.
Each level owns an independent codebook, and a de-duplication suffix is appended whenever two
items collide on all four levels, guaranteeing an injective item↔code mapping. A user history
x = {i1, . . . , in−1} is thus flattened into a token sequence of length 4(n −1), and predicting the next
item amounts to autoregressively generating its 4 semantic tokens. Note that the tokenization module
is not frozen: a candidate is free to re-fit or redesign the quantizer (e.g. changing the number of levels,
the codebook size or the quantization algorithm) as part of its proposed modification, in which case
the downstream backbone is retrained accordingly. Only the upstream interaction data and the splits
are fixed. The seed baselines reported in the main text all use the original configuration above.
Backbone. The seed backbone is TIGER (Rajput et al., 2023), a T5-style Transformer encoder-
decoder operating entirely in the semantic-token space. The encoder consumes the flattened history
tokens and the decoder autoregressively emits the 4 codes of the target item; at inference time
decoding is performed with constrained beam search over the valid code trie. Both the encoder and
the decoder consist of 4 layers with 6 self-attention heads of head dimension 64, ReLU activations
in all feed-forward blocks, and a learnable token embedding dimension of 128, yielding roughly
0.01B parameters in total. The full architectural and optimisation configuration is listed in Table 3;
all values are inherited from Yu et al. (2026) without modification.
Table 3: Architecture and optimisation configuration of the seed GR codebase. These values are
shared by the pre-training baseline and all post-training variants, and constitute the identical starting
point from which every evolutionary framework departs.

Pre-training Baseline. TIGER (Pre-train) (Rajput et al., 2023) optimises the standard token-level
cross-entropy (maximum-likelihood) objective under teacher forcing,

where y+ denotes the ground-truth code sequence. Every post-training variant below is initialised
from this converged checkpoint, so that the observed differences are attributable purely to the
post-training objective.
Post-training Variants. The seed codebase ships with four post-training objectives, which together
span the mainstream design space of preference- and reinforcement-based alignment for generative
recommendation. They constitute the algorithmic prior that the evolutionary frameworks may
recombine, ablate or extend.
• SDPO (Chen et al., 2024) generalises Direct Preference Optimization to a multi-negative, softmax-
weighted ranking loss. Given a positive item ei,+ and a sampled negative set N, it optimises
LSDPO = −log σ



,
(2)
where πref is the frozen pre-trained reference policy. Crucially, the preference signal is defined
at the complete sequence level, i.e. on the cumulative likelihood of the whole item, with a single
summation over N.
• SPRec (Gao et al., 2025) is a self-play framework designed to suppress the over-recommendation
/ filter-bubble bias that plain DPO induces. Each self-play iteration performs one SFT step on
the offline interactions followed by one DPO step in which the model’s own predictions from the
previous iteration serve as negatives. Because the negative distribution is the current policy’s own
output, the DPO loss is implicitly re-weighted by the model logits, adaptively penalising items the
model already over-exposes. No extra data or manual intervention is needed.
• ReReGRPO (Tan et al., 2025) casts post-training as reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
on top of GRPO. Two domain-specific adaptations make GRPO viable in the constrained item space:
(i) candidates are sampled by constrained beam search rather than i.i.d. sampling, which yields a
group of valid, distinct and on-policy hard negatives in a single pass; and (ii) the sparse binary rule
reward (exact match with the target) is augmented with a ranking reward that penalises a generated
negative proportionally to its probability rank, r(ek) = Rrule(ek) + λRrank(ek). Advantages
are normalised within the group, ˆAk = (rk −mean(r))/std(r), and a KL penalty towards the
reference policy stabilises the update.
• APAO (Yu et al., 2026) attacks the training-inference inconsistency directly by moving supervision
from the sequence level to every intermediate prefix. Defining the cumulative score of a length-m
prefix as sm = P
t≤m log πθ(yt | x, y<t), the pairwise variant optimises
Lpair = LCE + β

log-likelihood. The prefix weights w ∈∆T −1 are not fixed but follow an exponentiated-gradient
update, wm ←wm exp(ηLm) followed by re-normalisation, which realises adaptive worst-prefix
optimisation: the step whose prefix is currently most likely to fall out of the beam receives the
largest weight.
A.4
EVOLUTION BASELINES
We compare TGR-EvoDAG against six evolutionary frameworks, grouped into general evolutionary
frameworks (domain-agnostic) and recommender-specific frameworks (built for recommendation).
Every baseline is instantiated on the same seed codebase, executed by the same coding agent (Claude
CLI), and constrained by the same budget B = 24 GPU-hours described in the main text, so that the
differences reported stem from the search strategy itself rather than from the environment.
20


--- Page 21 ---
Preprint.
General evolutionary frameworks.
• AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) orchestrates an autonomous LLM-driven evolutionary pipeline
that iteratively evolves and optimizes entire algorithmic codebases by directly editing and testing
code against evaluator feedback. It generalizes the FunSearch/Eureka line of LLM-driven code
evolution from single functions to whole codebases, but is guided primarily by scalar metrics and
carries no recommendation-specific inductive bias.
• DeepEvolve (Liu et al., 2025b) extends the evolutionary loop with retrieval-augmented generation
(RAG): it retrieves external scientific knowledge (e.g., academic papers from arXiv) to systemati-
cally inform hypothesis generation and codebase refinement, grounding the evolution in prior work
rather than relying on the model’s internal knowledge alone.
• CORAL (Qu et al., 2026) is a multi-agent framework for open-ended discovery that replaces
rigid control flow with long-running agents that explore, reflect, and collaborate through a shared
persistent memory and asynchronous execution.
• Arbor (Jin et al., 2026) is a general autonomous-research framework built on Hypothesis Tree
Refinement : a persistent tree links hypotheses, artifacts, evidence, and distilled insights across time.
A long-lived coordinator manages the global strategy over the tree, while short-lived executors
implement and test individual hypotheses in isolated worktrees; returned results are propagated
back into the tree as reusable lessons that refine the search frontier.
Recommender-specific frameworks.
• EvoRec (Mu et al., 2026) is a multi-agent framework that co-evolves both the recommendation
model and the optimization methodology driving it. Four agents (an Orchestrator, a Research
Agent, a Code Agent, and a Skill Evolver) run a dual-track loop: the Research and Code agents
iterate the model each round, while the Skill Evolver periodically distills reusable methodology
from a persistent memory of past experiments into a self-evolving skill library. It is domain-aware
but is guided primarily by offline metrics, without the directional diagnosis.
• Self-EvolveRec (Kim et al., 2026) introduces directional feedback for recommender evolution,
pairing a User Simulator that emits natural-language critiques with a Model Diagnosis Tool that
probes internal structure (e.g., embedding collapse, ranking margin) and interprets the numbers
into a structured diagnosis. A Diagnosis Tool Co-Evolution mechanism keeps the diagnosis tool
compatible with the evolving model, and an evolutionary archive retains the codebase history.
A.5
MULTI-DIMENSION DIAGNOSTICS
During evolution the environment produces, for every executed candidate, a structured feedback
bundle assembled from three complementary diagnostic channels, following the directional-feedback
design of Self-EvolveRec (Kim et al., 2026) (which pairs a qualitative User Simulator with a
quantitative Model Diagnosis Tool) and specialising it to the 4-layer semantic-ID (SID) generative
recommender. The three channels are: (i) offline validation metrics, giving a macro-level view
of ranking quality; (ii) deterministic mathematical probes, exposing internal failure modes that
aggregate metrics cannot express; and (iii) qualitative user diagnosis, surfacing behaviour-level
deficiencies in natural language. While offline metrics in Channel (i) are available to every framework,
diagnostic feedback in Channels (ii) and (iii) is provided exclusively to domain-specific methods,
naive integration variants (Arbor + Diag. and CORAL + Diag.), and TGR-EvoDAG. For these
methods, the diagnostic content is emitted stage-aware: the bundle carries separate fields for the
supervised-fine-tuning stage (sft_*) and the post-training stage (post_*), so that multi-stage
diagnostics are produced only if a candidate actually modifies post-training; a single-stage candidate
(e.g., pure TIGER) receives only the sft_* fields.
Channel (i): Offline validation metrics.
The environment computes standard ranking metrics
(Hit@K and NDCG@K, K ∈{10, 20}) on the validation set via constrained beam search (beam
size 20), as formalised in Appendix A.6. These scalars quantify how well the candidate ranks,
but not why it fails, and are therefore complemented by the two channels below. In the feedback
bundle the metrics appear both as the final-model value (offline_val) and as the per-stage values
(sft_stage_val, post_stage_val) to enable stage-level credit assignment.
21


--- Page 22 ---
Preprint.
Channel (ii): Deterministic mathematical probes.
The probe suite deterministically measures
structural and decoding properties of the trained model, and is grouped into four families summarised
in Table 4. All values are computed by the environment on the validation split; the baseline probe set
is fixed and cannot be altered by any framework.
Probe extensibility.
Although the baseline probe set is fixed, a candidate is permitted to imple-
ment and upload additional probe scripts to broaden its own diagnostic coverage. The environ-
ment merges candidate-contributed metrics into the baseline under an agent.* namespace and
enforces an additive-only policy (candidate probes may not overwrite baseline probes), so the offi-
cial diagnostic surface remains identical across frameworks while a framework may still monitor
candidate-specific signals. The execution status of any submitted probe is reported back in the
sft_probe_fn_status / post_probe_fn_status fields.
Table 4: The four families of deterministic mathematical probes. Each probe yields one or more
numeric values (indexed by SID layer or popularity tier) and targets a specific internal failure mode
of generative recommendation.

The raw numeric values are not fed to the coding agent directly. Instead, an LLM-based Diagnosis
Analyst interprets them into a structured diagnosis following the schema of Table 5; the prompt
instructs the analyst to ignore any conclusion-inducing wording, to ground every statement in a
named metric and its value, and to populate the headline_metrics field with the 3-6 numeric
values that most directly support the verdict (making the diagnosis auditable).
Channel (iii): Qualitative user diagnosis.
Following the user-simulator paradigm in Self-
EvolveRec (Kim et al., 2026), we instantiate an LLM-based simulator to produce behaviour-level
22


--- Page 23 ---
Preprint.
critiques. We construct a population of simulated users, each governed by a fixed persona spanning
three traits (activity, conformity, and diversity, each ranging from LOW to HIGH). Conditioned on
their individual interaction histories, these simulated users evaluate the candidate’s top-K recommen-
dations via a two-step protocol:
• Item-level Assessment: The simulator inspects each recommended item to predict the user’s
reaction. It outputs a binary verdict (align/misalign) along with a short causal reasoning for the
decision.
• List-level Feedback: Building on the item verdicts, the simulator abstracts the overall quality of
the top-K list. It identifies which decision signals the model correctly captured, which patterns
were overgeneralized, and which user intentions were missed.
Finally, to mitigate individual-user bias and surface systematic flaws, a global aggregator (prompted as
a Lead Analyst) synthesizes all per-user reports. This yields a single, macro-level system critique that
strictly adheres to the unified StandardDiagnosis schema, serving as the qualitative counterpart
to the mathematical probes.
Unified diagnosis schema.
Both the mathematical and the qualitative channels converge on a single
schema (Table 5), so that the coding agent consumes one uniform diagnostic interface regardless of
which channel produced the content.

diagnostic channels.

A.6
METRICS
In this section, we will introduce offline recommendation metrics (Hit and NDCG) as well as metrics
defined in Agent4rec that simulate user experience.
Offline Recommendation Metrics. Under the leave-one-out protocol each user u has exactly one
ground-truth next item i∗
u. Given the ranked list Ru of length K produced by constrained beam
search, let ranku ∈{1, . . . , K} ∪{∞} denote the position of i∗
u in Ru (ranku = ∞if it is not
retrieved).

We report K ∈{10, 20}. Since the beam size equals 20, the top-20 list is exactly the beam-search
output, and the top-10 list is its truncation.
Agent4Rec Metrics. Offline recommendation metrics summarise a single next-item prediction and
are therefore blind to list-level behavioural effects such as over-concentration. To complement them,
we additionally report three behaviour-level metrics obtained from the LLM-based user simulator
Agent4Rec (Zhang et al., 2024). In this simulator each generative agent is initialised from a real
user profile (activity, conformity and diversity traits) and interacts with the evaluated recommender
page by page: four items are displayed per page, the agent chooses which items to view and rates
them on a 1-5 scale, and then decides whether to request the next page or to exit, being forced to exit
after at most five pages. A rating higher than 3 is treated as a like. Let A denote the evaluation agent
population, and for agent a let Ea be the number of exposed items, La the number of liked items,
and pa ∈[1, 5] the page index at which a exits. We report
¯Plike =
1
|A|
X
a∈A
La
Ea
,
¯Nlike =
1
|A|
X
a∈A
La,
¯Nexit =
1
|A|
X
a∈A
pa.
(7)
Higher values indicate a better simulated user experience for all three metrics. ¯Plike measures the
precision of the exposed list at the behaviour level, ¯Nlike measures the absolute volume of satisfied
interests a session delivers, and ¯Nexit measures engagement depth: a larger exit page indicates the
agent kept browsing rather than abandoning the session early.
Agent4Rec metrics are used strictly for evaluation. They are computed only once, on the single
checkpoint finally retained under the budget B, and serve exclusively to compare the frameworks
in the main results table. They are never computed for intermediate candidates, never exposed to any
evolving framework, and never used for model selection. Model selection relies solely on the offline
24


--- Page 25 ---
Preprint.
validation metrics defined above. Consequently, no framework can optimise these numbers directly,
and they function as a genuinely held-out behavioural measurement.
We stress that this evaluation simulator is fully disjoint from the user simulator that supplies the
third feedback channel during evolution. The latter follows the qualitative-diagnosis design of Self-
EvolveRec (Kim et al., 2026) and emits natural-language diagnostic reports (Appendix A.5) rather
than scalar scores. The two components are isolated along two axes: (i) the user populations are
drawn from disjoint user sets, so no agent that participates in evolution-time diagnosis is ever reused
for final measurement; and (ii) their outputs are of different kinds and consumed by different parties:
diagnostic text is consumed by the coding agent during the search, whereas the three metrics above
are consumed only by us, after the search terminates. This separation rules out any feedback path
from the evaluation protocol back into the evolutionary process. Within the evaluation simulator
itself, the agent population, the random seeds and the interaction templates are fixed once and shared
by all frameworks, so the reported comparison is deterministic and paired.
